proposed_node.title: Mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control
proposed_node.canonical_question: What is mitophagy and how are damaged mitochondria targeted for degradation?
proposed_node.summary: Mitophagy is the selective autophagy of damaged mitochondria. The PINK1-Parkin pathway detects depolarised mitochondria and tags them with ubiquitin, recruiting autophagy receptors that deliver the mitochondrion to a lysosome for digestion.

sections.heading: What is mitophagy?
sections.body: Mitophagy is the selective removal of damaged or surplus mitochondria by the cell's recycling system, autophagy. The word combines 'mito' (mitochondrion) and 'phagy' (eating). Rather than letting a faulty mitochondrion linger and produce harmful reactive oxygen species, the cell wraps it in a double-membrane sac called an autophagosome and delivers it to a lysosome, where digestive enzymes break everything down for reuse.

sections.heading: How does the cell recognise a damaged mitochondrion?
sections.body:
The key signal is loss of the electrochemical gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane (the membrane potential). A healthy mitochondrion maintains this gradient to drive ATP synthesis. When a mitochondrion is damaged, the gradient collapses.

A protein kinase called PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1) is the sensor. In healthy mitochondria, PINK1 is imported into the inner membrane and quickly degraded, so it never builds up. When the membrane potential drops, import stalls and PINK1 accumulates on the outer membrane instead.

sections.heading: How PINK1 recruits Parkin to tag the mitochondrion
sections.body:
Accumulated PINK1 on the outer membrane phosphorylates ubiquitin and a cytosolic E3 ubiquitin ligase called Parkin. These phosphorylation events activate Parkin, which then attaches ubiquitin chains to many proteins on the mitochondrial surface. This ubiquitin coating acts as an 'eat me' flag.

Autophagy receptor proteins such as p62/SQSTM1, NDP52, and OPTN recognise the ubiquitin chains. These receptors also bind LC3, a protein on the growing autophagosome membrane, physically tethering the tagged mitochondrion to the autophagosome.

sections.heading: Delivery to the lysosome and digestion
sections.body:
Once enclosed in an autophagosome, the mitochondrion is transported along microtubules to a lysosome. The two membranes fuse, and lysosomal enzymes (proteases, lipases, nucleases) break down the mitochondrial contents into amino acids, fatty acids, and nucleotides that can be reused by the cell.

The whole sequence from membrane-potential collapse to completed digestion can take a few hours in a typical mammalian cell.

sections.heading: Why mitophagy matters for health
sections.body: Mutations in PINK1 and Parkin are among the most common genetic causes of early-onset Parkinson's disease, highlighting how important mitochondrial quality control is in neurons, which cannot simply divide to dilute damaged organelles. Defective mitophagy allows ROS-producing mitochondria to accumulate, contributing to cell death in several neurodegenerative conditions.

rendering.audience_note: Written at an introductory level for a 16-18 or adult learner with no prior knowledge of autophagy assumed. Technical terms are defined on first use.
